title: Writing a Polynomial from Its Zeros
short: Multiply factors for each zero, including complex pairs, and scale to fit a point.
trouble: Students write x + 3 as the factor for the zero 3, or leave out the conjugate of a complex zero.

blocks.html: Now run the factor theorem backwards: from the zeros, build the polynomial. Remember from the The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra that complex zeros of real polynomials come in pairs.

Each zero $r$ gives a factor $(x - r)$. Multiply the factors, multiply by a constant $a$, and use any extra point to find $a$. Multiply conjugate or $\pm\sqrt{m}$ pairs first: $(x - (p + qi))(x - (p - qi))$ $= (x - p)^2 + q^2$ and $(x - \sqrt{m})(x + \sqrt{m}) = x^2 - m$.

By the factor theorem, $p(r) = 0$ exactly when $(x - r)$ divides $p(x)$, so a polynomial with all those zeros must contain all those factors. Any constant multiple has the same zeros, so a point off the axis is needed to choose the one you want. Pairing conjugates first keeps the arithmetic real: it is the difference of squares $(x - p)^2 - (qi)^2$, and $i^2 = -1$ turns the minus into a plus.

blocks.title: A complex zero
blocks.q: Find the polynomial of lowest degree with real coefficients, leading coefficient 1, and zeros $2$ and $1 + 3i$.
steps: $1 - 3i$ is also a zero, so the degree is 3.

blocks.html: Writing $(x + 3)$ for the zero $3$. A zero $r$ needs a factor that is 0 at $r$, which is $(x - r)$. Check: $(3) - 3 = 0$. Also include the conjugate of every complex zero, or the coefficients will not be real.
